preamble: The first line of a limerick (1,7,3,4,2,9) is to be written in the numbered squares, 1 to 26, in order. The words of the remaining four lines of the limerick may be found, in order, in the first nine clues. The other clues are listed in alphabetical order of their solutions and are numbered for reference only. All solutions must be fitted into the diagram jigsaw-wise. Because of the symmetry there are two possible ways of doing this, so please check that your limerick starts at 1 and not 7!

clue.text: Content of a hive with model at its centre in a town

definitions.text: Content of a hive with model at its centre in a town

indicators.note: something placed at the centre of the town sits inside that word's letters

parts.note: the article taken as written
a city is a large town
the Model T was Ford's famous car

indicators.note: the content of something is what sits inside it, so only the inner letters of hive are kept

parts.note: the two inner letters of hive

explanation.surface: A busy hive of bees sits in the middle of a town, with a model on display.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: a hive is full of busy work. Model T is Ford's famous early car.
explanation.definitionFit: A hive is proverbially full of busy work, as in the idiom 'a hive of industry', so what fills it is bustle.

clue.text: Numbered request: can I hold my liquor?

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, so a numbered letter
to ask is to request

explanation.surface: A drinker politely asks whether they can still manage their drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'can' as a noun: the container speaks, saying it holds liquor; the drinker's worry is the false picture.
explanation.definitionFit: A cask is a wooden barrel that stores wine, beer or spirits, so it is a vessel speaking of its contents.

clue.text: 'E was a brave man, not quite dead, just worn away

indicators.note: not quite whole means the word falls a letter short of complete

parts.note: a brave man is a hero; the dropped H of 'E tells us to drop it here too, Cockney style
dead with its A removed

explanation.surface: A Cockney tribute to a brave man who is nearly dead and quite worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ERO (hero without its H) plus DED gives ERODED; the apostrophe in 'E is the hint to drop an H.
explanation.definitionFit: Rock or soil that has eroded has been gradually ground down by water, wind or weather.

clue.text: Read only memory to reply (say) to the writer of novels

parts.note: ROM is the abbreviation for read-only memory

indicators.note: say means as spoken, so the reply is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: a reply is an answer, spoken in the southern English way

explanation.surface: A computer's memory is asked to talk back to a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: In southern British speech 'answer' rhymes with the end of ROMANCER, so ROM plus that sound gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A romancer is one who writes romances, the old term for long prose stories of adventure and love.

clue.text: Badly rattled battler pretty affected by awful muddle

indicators.note: something awful is a mess, so the letters are left in disorder

parts.note: twee means affectedly pretty or quaint
the letters of muddle rearranged

explanation.surface: A fighter is badly shaken, prettily posturing and thrown by a dreadful muddle.
explanation.walkthrough: In Through the Looking-Glass, Tweedledum agrees to battle Tweedledee, but both flee when a monstrous crow frightens them.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll's quarrelsome twin agreed to fight his brother, then was frightened off by a crow, a famous scared combatant.

clue.text: Almost every copper at home to Charlemagne's mentor

indicators.note: almost means nearly but not wholly, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: every is all, cut short by a letter
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
someone at home is in

explanation.surface: Nearly every policeman is at home to receive the Emperor Charlemagne's teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' is British slang for a policeman, but here it is the metal, symbol CU.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcuin of York was the English scholar who taught at Charlemagne's court and led his revival of learning.

clue.text: Image containing pear-shaped protection for bridge in winter

indicators.note: in British slang a plan that goes pear-shaped goes wrong, so these letters end up out of order
containing means the first word wraps around the other letters

parts.note: an icon is an image
the letters of pear rearranged

explanation.surface: A picture holds a pear-shaped object, which turns out to shield a bridge in winter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pear-shaped' reads as a description of the protection; its job is to scramble pear.
explanation.definitionFit: An ice apron is a sloping structure placed upstream of a bridge pier to break up floating ice.

clue.text: Number considered partly to finish a game

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, the call that ends a game

indicators.note: partly means only part of the next word survives, with letters cut from both its ends

parts.note: No. is the abbreviation for number
taken as written, then trimmed of CON and RED

explanation.surface: A number is mulled over in deciding how to end a game.
explanation.walkthrough: No-side is the referee's call ending a rugby match.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby the referee calls no-side when time is up and the match ends.

clue.text: Author wins the gold before spring

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry
a well is a spring of water

explanation.surface: A writer takes the gold medal ahead of the spring season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' suggests the season; here it is a source of water.
explanation.definitionFit: George Orwell wrote Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four, so he is an example of a writer.

clue.text: Singular course off the cuff?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a golf course is called ..., so one of them is the singular
second meaning: what a cufflink is, read as coming off the cuff

explanation.walkthrough: 'Off the cuff' looks like the idiom for unrehearsed; the question mark says read it literally, as a piece from a cufflink. Links is a seaside golf course.
explanation.definitionFit: Links is a seaside golf course, so one is its singular; a cufflink also fastens a shirt cuff.

clue.text: Infected when various uses failed

indicators.note: various suggests different arrangements, so the following letters are rearranged

parts.note: all ten letters of the two words rearranged

explanation.surface: Something became infected after several attempted uses went wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Diseaseful is a rare word for full of disease, so it describes something infected or diseased.

clue.text: 'Urley uneasy — could be a monitor

parts.note: Liz Hurley is the British actress and model; her first name stands for her
un-easy is hard, and the dropped H of 'Urley says to drop the H here too

explanation.surface: Someone called Hurley, said in a Cockney accent, is nervous about being watched on a screen.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'Urley marks a dropped H, so 'ard is hard said the same way; LIZ plus ARD gives LIZARD.
explanation.definitionFit: A monitor is a large tropical reptile, such as the Komodo dragon, so it is one example of the creature.

clue.text: Everyone first has audible spats with the beasts one sees afterwards

parts.note: everyone is all

indicators.note: audible means as heard, so the word for spats is taken by its sound

parts.note: spats are short gaiters covering the ankle

explanation.surface: Everybody arrives in noisy footwear, alongside animals seen at a later time.
explanation.walkthrough: Said aloud, 'all gaiters' sounds like ALLIGATORS. The definition rests on the parting phrase 'See you later, alligator'.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyming farewell 'See you later, alligator' makes those reptiles creatures one sees afterwards.

clue.text: Link up in space and come down to earth by modern light railway?

parts.note: spacecraft dock when they join up in orbit
to land is to come down to the ground

explanation.surface: A spacecraft links up in orbit, then returns to earth and takes the train.
explanation.walkthrough: The Docklands Light Railway is a modern driverless railway serving London's old docks area.
explanation.definitionFit: London's redeveloped docks area is served by the Docklands Light Railway, so it is reached that way.

clue.text: Craven ribbon?

definitions.note: an example: the colour of a famous ribbon
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the colour of the ribbon of song, tied as a sign of welcome home

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that the second sense is by example: a yellow ribbon is the famous token of waiting for someone's return.
explanation.definitionFit: Yellow is slang for cowardly, and it is the colour of the ribbon tied round the old oak tree in the song.

clue.text: Betty Boothroyd (will there ever be another?) having some golden hair?

definitions.text: Betty Boothroyd (will there ever be another?)

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry
a, as in a certain amount
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: A famous politician, unique in her role, is pictured with some golden hair.
explanation.walkthrough: Betty Boothroyd was the first woman Speaker of the House of Commons; the bracket wonders whether there will be another woman Speaker, or whether the old word will be used again.
explanation.definitionFit: An oratress is an archaic word for a female orator or speaker, fitting the first woman Speaker of the Commons.

clue.text: Domestic appliance London shop can't quite sell?

indicators.note: the shop cannot have the word, and not quite all of it, so a shortened form is taken away

parts.note: Selfridges is the big Oxford Street department store in London
sell short of its last letter

explanation.surface: A household appliance that a London store somehow cannot manage to sell.
explanation.walkthrough: SELFRIDGE minus SEL leaves FRIDGE.
explanation.definitionFit: A fridge, short for refrigerator, is a household machine that keeps food cold.

clue.text: A German saint and a German thinker

parts.note: ein is German for a
St is the abbreviation for saint
the German word for a once more

explanation.surface: A list of two German figures: a holy saint and a philosopher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A German' is read as the German word for 'a', not as a German person; the second one also tells you the thinker is German.
explanation.definitionFit: Albert Einstein, born in Ulm, was the physicist whose theories of relativity reshaped science, a great mind.

clue.text: Add a thanksgiving put in at church

indicators.note: put in means placed inside, so the thanks go within the other letters

parts.note: taken as written
ta is British informal for thanks
CH is the abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: Someone adds a prayer of thanks during a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: AT CH holds TA: AT(TA)CH. 'Ta' is a casual British thank-you.
explanation.definitionFit: To attach something is to fasten or join it on, so to append or include it.

clue.text: Male grandparent has little time and is making no progress

parts.note: a stag is a male deer
nan is a familiar name for a grandmother
t is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: An old grandfather has little time left and is getting nowhere.
explanation.definitionFit: Stagnant describes water that does not flow, and by extension an economy or career that does not develop.

clue.text: What's caused by a bore? Tide turning and… let me think…

indicators.note: something turning changes its position, so these letters are moved about

parts.note: the letters of tide rearranged
um is the noise of someone pausing to think

explanation.surface: A tidal bore rolls up the river as the tide turns, while someone hesitates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bore' and 'tide' together suggest a tidal wave up a river; here the bore is a dull person.
explanation.definitionFit: Tedium is weariness and boredom, the feeling produced by a dull, tiresome person.

clue.text: A plate for my beastly back!

indicators.note: back means going the other way, so the word is read from its end

parts.note: beastly as an adjective means animal

explanation.surface: Someone wants a protective plate for their creature's back.
explanation.definitionFit: A lamina is a thin layer or sheet of material, so a thin plate of bone, metal or rock.

clue.text: She is embraced by a boy and severely criticised

indicators.note: being embraced means being held inside someone's arms, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: a lad is a boy
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman is hugged by a young man, then given a harsh dressing-down.
explanation.definitionFit: To lash someone verbally is to attack them with harsh words, so a scathing rebuke.

clue.text: Leaders to lead — or is it a new arrangement?

indicators.note: a new arrangement of the words means their letters are placed in a different order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether giving leaders the lead is a fresh arrangement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaders' suggests people in charge; here it means newspaper leaders, the British term for editorial articles.
explanation.definitionFit: A leader, or leading article, is a newspaper's opinion piece giving the paper's own view.

clue.text: Small letter

definitions.note: adjective; the answer is a noun for a very small amount

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a character of the Greek alphabet

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a lower-case character; the two words are separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The ninth Greek character is the smallest in form, so the word has come to mean a tiny quantity.

clue.text: Boy goes first to the front

parts.note: I is one in Roman numerals, the first number
the van is the front of an army or procession

explanation.surface: A boy marches first, up to the head of the line.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivan is the Russian form of John, a common masculine given name.

clue.text: Changeable regiments?

parts.note: surface reading: fickle, unreliable soldiers
setter's reading: the household troops whose daily changing at Buckingham Palace is a ceremony

explanation.walkthrough: 'Changeable' suggests inconstant; it means able to be changed, as in the Changing of the Guard at Buckingham Palace.
explanation.definitionFit: The Guards are the British Army's household regiments, famous for their sentry handover ceremony in London.

clue.text: Sounds of Priestley in the upper room?

indicators.note: sounds means the phrase that follows is heard, not spelt

parts.note: an attic is the room at the top of a house, and the upper one is higher

explanation.surface: Noises from the writer J. B. Priestley come down from a room upstairs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Priestley' looks like the playwright's name but is to be read as the adjective priestly.
explanation.definitionFit: Hieratic means relating to priests, as in the cursive script once used by Egyptian priests.
